questions.question: What is the difference between Authentication and Authorization in Spring Security?
questions.title: Authentication vs Authorization in Spring Security
questions.direct_answer: Authentication answers 'Who are you?' — it verifies identity by checking credentials and produces an Authentication object stored in the SecurityContext. Authorization answers 'What are you allowed to do?' — it checks the authenticated principal's authorities against the required permissions for a resource. Spring Security enforces these as two distinct, sequential steps.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can clearly articulate the two-step security model and map it to Spring Security's concrete types.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Conflating the two concepts, or not knowing that Authorization can only work after Authentication populates the SecurityContext.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Reference the Authentication interface, GrantedAuthority, AuthenticationManager, and AccessDecisionManager (or the newer AuthorizationManager in Spring Security 6).

sections.title: Authentication Establishes WHO You Are — Authorization Determines WHAT You Can Do
sections.content:
The two concepts are sequential: **authentication must happen before authorization can work.** You cannot decide what a user is allowed to do until you know who they are. Conflating them is the most common mistake in security interviews — and it leads to real bugs like returning 403 to unauthenticated users, which tells attackers the resource exists.

In Spring Security, **authentication** is handled by `AuthenticationManager`, which delegates to one or more `AuthenticationProvider` implementations. The result is an `Authentication` object stored in the `SecurityContextHolder`. This object carries three things: the principal (who), the credentials (proof of identity, usually cleared after success), and a collection of `GrantedAuthority` objects representing roles and permissions.

**Authorization** uses those `GrantedAuthority` values to make access decisions. The `AuthorizationManager` — which replaced the older `AccessDecisionManager` in Spring Security 6 — evaluates whether the authenticated principal holds the required authority for the requested resource. Authorization can happen at two layers: URL-level (in the filter chain via `requestMatchers().hasRole()`) and method-level (`@PreAuthorize` with SpEL). URL-level is faster and coarser. Method-level is finer-grained and can inspect method arguments and return values.

The **401 vs 403 distinction** is the clearest signal of whether you understand this. A 401 means "I don't know who you are — provide credentials." A 403 means "I know who you are, but you're not allowed." Returning 403 for an unauthenticated request leaks information about the resource's existence. Spring Security handles this correctly by default: `AuthenticationEntryPoint` sends 401 for unauthenticated requests and `AccessDeniedHandler` sends 403 for authenticated-but-unauthorized requests.

sections.title: Authentication vs Authorization — Mechanism, Timing, and Spring Components
sections.content:
The distinction maps directly to different Spring Security components with different responsibilities.

| Aspect | Authentication | Authorization |
|---|---|---|
| **Question** | Who are you? | What can you do? |
| **When** | First — before any access decision | After — requires authenticated principal |
| **Failure response** | 401 Unauthorized | 403 Forbidden |
| **Spring component** | `AuthenticationManager` / `AuthenticationProvider` | `AuthorizationManager` / `@PreAuthorize` |
| **Data produced** | `Authentication` object (principal + credentials) | Access decision (allow or deny) |
| **Input** | Credentials (username/password, token, certificate) | `GrantedAuthority` collection + required permission |
| **Storage** | `SecurityContextHolder` (ThreadLocal per request) | Evaluated per request — not stored |
| **Configuration** | `UserDetailsService`, OAuth2, LDAP, SAML | `requestMatchers().hasRole()`, `@PreAuthorize` |

**`GrantedAuthority` is the bridge** between the two phases. Whatever roles you attach during authentication become the vocabulary that authorization rules consume. A `GrantedAuthority` with value `ROLE_ADMIN` attached during login is what makes `hasRole("ADMIN")` return true later. If the roles aren't attached correctly during authentication, every authorization check fails — and the symptom looks like a broken authorization rule when the actual bug is in the authentication phase.

sections.title: URL-Level vs Method-Level Authorization — Choosing the Right Enforcement Point
sections.content:
URL-level authorization (configured in `SecurityFilterChain` with `requestMatchers("/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")`) applies to entire endpoint groups and runs at the filter layer — before any application code executes. This is the fastest line of defense: obviously unauthorized requests are rejected before they consume application resources.

Method-level authorization (`@PreAuthorize`, `@PostAuthorize`) handles fine-grained rules that depend on domain data. "Only the owner can delete their own post" cannot be expressed as a URL pattern — the post ID is in the path, and evaluating ownership requires a repository lookup. `@PreAuthorize("#post.authorId == authentication.principal.id")` performs this check with access to method parameters.

**Use both layers together.** URL rules reject obviously unauthorized requests early. Method-level annotations enforce the ownership and attribute-based checks that URL patterns cannot. The common mistake is relying only on URL-level rules and assuming they're sufficient — a single wildcard misconfiguration can expose an entire section of the API. Defense in depth means `@PreAuthorize` provides a second check even if the URL rule is misconfigured or bypassed.

One practical pattern: configure URL rules broadly (`authenticated()`) and enforce specific role and ownership constraints with method-level annotations. This separates authentication enforcement (URL level) from fine-grained authorization logic (method level), making both easier to audit and test.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Authentication answers 'who are you?'; authorization answers 'what are you allowed to do?'** — authentication must succeed before authorization is evaluated; a 401 means unauthenticated, a 403 means authenticated but unauthorized.
- **`Authentication` object holds the principal and authorities** — after successful authentication, Spring stores an `Authentication` in the `SecurityContext`; `getAuthorities()` returns `GrantedAuthority` objects checked by authorization.
- **`AuthenticationManager` delegates to `AuthenticationProvider` chain** — `DaoAuthenticationProvider` is the default; it loads `UserDetails` from `UserDetailsService` and verifies the password with `PasswordEncoder`.
- **Authorization is evaluated after authentication in the filter chain** — `AuthorizationFilter` (or `FilterSecurityInterceptor`) runs after the authentication filter; checking authorization before authentication completes is not possible.
- **Method security (`@PreAuthorize`) is a second authorization layer** — HTTP security rules protect endpoints; `@PreAuthorize` protects service methods; both can be active simultaneously for defense in depth.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Authentication and authorization are two distinct steps in security. Conflating them is the most common conceptual error in security interviews.

**Authentication — identity verification**
- 'Who are you?' — the user presents credentials (username/password, JWT, certificate)
- Spring's `AuthenticationManager` verifies the credentials
- On success, an `Authentication` object is stored in the `SecurityContextHolder` — containing the principal and their `GrantedAuthority` list
- Failure → `AuthenticationException` → `401 Unauthorized`

**Authorization — permission check**
- 'What are you allowed to do?' — evaluated after authentication succeeds
- Spring checks the `GrantedAuthority` list against the required role/permission for the requested resource
- Failure → `AccessDeniedException` → `403 Forbidden`

**The Spring Security flow**
- Request enters the filter chain
- Authentication filter (e.g., `UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter`) extracts credentials and calls `AuthenticationManager`
- `DaoAuthenticationProvider` loads `UserDetails` via `UserDetailsService`, verifies password with `PasswordEncoder`
- On success, stores `Authentication` in `SecurityContextHolder`
- `AuthorizationFilter` checks `SecurityContextHolder` against the required authorities for the URL

`@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")` on service methods adds a second authorization layer — even if someone bypasses the HTTP-level check, the method-level check still enforces the permission.

questions.question: How does the Spring Security filter chain work, and in what order do requests flow through it?
questions.title: Spring Security Filter Chain — How Requests Flow Through
questions.direct_answer: The Spring Security filter chain is a series of servlet filters that intercept every HTTP request before it reaches your controller. Each filter performs a specific security task — from reading credentials to checking authorities — and the chain halts early if a request fails any check. Filters are ordered so that credential extraction always happens before authorization decisions.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands that Spring Security is filter-based and can reason about ordering and short-circuit behavior.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking Spring Security hooks into the controller layer — it operates entirely at the servlet filter level, before DispatcherServlet.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention FilterChainProxy, SecurityFilterChain beans, and how multiple chains can match different URL patterns with different configurations.

sections.title: Spring Security Operates Entirely at the Servlet Filter Level — Controllers Never See Unauthenticated Requests
sections.content:
The most important architectural fact about Spring Security: **it works as a servlet filter chain, not at the controller level.** By the time a request reaches your `@RestController`, authentication and authorization have already happened. If the request is rejected, the controller method never executes — it never even runs. Developers who think Spring Security intercepts inside Spring MVC are surprised when they discover that a custom `HandlerInterceptor` added for logging runs after Spring Security has already made its decision.

Spring Security registers a single `DelegatingFilterProxy` in the servlet container. This proxy looks up `FilterChainProxy` from the Spring `ApplicationContext` on the first request. `FilterChainProxy` holds one or more `SecurityFilterChain` beans — each matching a URL pattern and containing an ordered list of security filters. A request to `/api/**` might hit one chain with JWT authentication, while `/admin/**` hits another with form login and stricter rate limiting.

**The filter order within a chain is critical and fixed by Spring Security.** `SecurityContextHolderFilter` runs first to restore the security context. Authentication filters like `UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter` and `BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter` run in the middle — they attempt to authenticate the request and store the result in `SecurityContextHolder`. `ExceptionTranslationFilter` wraps the tail of the chain to catch authentication and access-denied exceptions. `AuthorizationFilter` runs last and evaluates access rules.

Inserting a custom filter at the wrong position breaks the security model in non-obvious ways. A custom authentication filter placed after `AuthorizationFilter` means every request is rejected before the custom filter ever runs. Spring Security provides `addFilterBefore()`, `addFilterAfter()`, and `addFilterAt()` to control placement precisely — understanding the chain order is what makes those calls meaningful rather than guesswork.

sections.title: How FilterChainProxy Selects and Executes the Right Chain
sections.content:
When a request enters `FilterChainProxy`, it iterates through its `SecurityFilterChain` beans in registration order and selects the **first chain whose `RequestMatcher` matches the URL.** This first-match behavior is critical: if a permissive chain (e.g., matching `/**`) is registered before a more specific one (e.g., matching `/api/**`), the specific chain never fires.

Spring Boot uses `@Order` to control chain priority. Lower order values run first. A JWT-authenticated API chain for `/api/**` should have a lower order number (higher priority) than the session-based web chain for `/**`. The ordering mistake is subtle because both chains might work individually — the bug appears only when the fallback chain catches API requests first and forces form login on your REST endpoints.

Within the selected chain, filters execute in a fixed sequence established by Spring Security's `FilterOrderRegistration`. Each filter calls `chain.doFilter()` to continue, or sends a response directly to halt the chain. **Authentication filters short-circuit on failure** — `BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter` rejects invalid tokens immediately by throwing `AuthenticationException`. `ExceptionTranslationFilter` catches this and sends the 401 response without the request ever reaching `AuthorizationFilter`.

Enable `spring.security.debug=true` in development to log every filter that executes per request. It prints each filter's class name and execution order, making the chain visible rather than inferred. Never enable this in production — it logs sensitive security data.

sections.title: Authentication Filters, ExceptionTranslationFilter, and AuthorizationFilter — The Critical Ordering
sections.content:
Understanding which filters do what — and why order matters — is what separates a developer who configures Spring Security mechanically from one who understands it.

**`SecurityContextHolderFilter`** runs first. For session-based auth, it loads the `SecurityContext` from the HTTP session into `SecurityContextHolder`, restoring the authenticated principal from the previous request. For stateless JWT APIs, it creates a new empty context. This must run before any authentication filter — `SecurityContextHolder.getContext()` returns a properly initialized (if empty) context only after this filter runs.

**Authentication filters** run next. Only one of these typically matches per request: `UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter` handles POST to `/login` with form parameters; `BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter` (from the OAuth2 Resource Server module) handles `Authorization: Bearer ...` headers. When authentication succeeds, the filter sets the `Authentication` in the `SecurityContext`. When it fails, it throws `AuthenticationException`.

**`ExceptionTranslationFilter`** wraps the remaining filters in a try-catch. It catches `AuthenticationException` (sends 401 or redirects to login depending on configuration) and `AccessDeniedException` (sends 403 or redirects to error page). Without this filter, authentication and authorization exceptions would propagate as unhandled exceptions and manifest as 500 errors.

**`AuthorizationFilter`** runs last. It evaluates `requestMatchers` rules and throws `AccessDeniedException` if the principal lacks the required authority. Moving this filter earlier doesn't improve performance — it means authorization runs before authentication has populated the principal, and every request fails.

sections.title: Custom Filter Insertion — Position Is a Security Decision, Not Just a Config Choice
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Spring Security is entirely filter-based — it operates before `DispatcherServlet`** — all security checks happen in `FilterChainProxy`, which delegates to the matching `SecurityFilterChain`.
- **Multiple `SecurityFilterChain` beans can coexist, matched by request pattern** — one chain for `/api/**` (stateless JWT), another for `/admin/**` (session-based); `@Order` determines priority.
- **Filter order within a chain is fixed by `FilterOrderRegistration`** — security filters have defined positions; inserting a custom filter uses `addFilterBefore`, `addFilterAfter`, or `addFilterAt`.
- **`UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter` handles form login; `BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter` handles JWTs** — the filter that runs depends on which authentication mechanism is configured.
- **`http.authorizeHttpRequests()` configures the `AuthorizationFilter`** — the last security filter in the chain; it reads the `SecurityContext` and checks the required authorities for the matched URL.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring Security's filter chain is the entire security layer. Understanding it means understanding what executes, in what order, before your controller ever sees the request.

**`FilterChainProxy`**
- Spring Security registers one `DelegatingFilterProxy` with the Servlet container
- It delegates to `FilterChainProxy`, which holds multiple `SecurityFilterChain` beans
- Each `SecurityFilterChain` has a request matcher (`/api/**`) and an ordered list of security filters

**Key filters in order**
- `SecurityContextHolderFilter` — loads the `SecurityContext` from the session (or creates empty)
- `UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter` — handles form login POST
- `BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter` — handles `Authorization: Bearer` JWTs
- `ExceptionTranslationFilter` — converts `AuthenticationException` → `401`, `AccessDeniedException` → `403`
- `AuthorizationFilter` — the last check: verifies the principal has the required authority for the URL

**Multiple chains**
- Define multiple `SecurityFilterChain` `@Bean` methods with `@Order`
- The chain whose `requestMatcher` matches first is used; subsequent chains are skipped
- Pattern: `@Order(1)` for `/api/**` (stateless, no session); `@Order(2)` for `/**` (session-based UI)

questions.question: How do SecurityContext and SecurityContextHolder work internally in Spring Security?
questions.title: SecurityContext and SecurityContextHolder — How They Work
questions.direct_answer: SecurityContextHolder is a static class that stores the current SecurityContext using a ThreadLocal (by default), making the authenticated user's Authentication accessible anywhere in the request-processing thread without passing it as a parameter. The SecurityContext holds a single Authentication object that is populated by authentication filters and cleared after the response is sent.

interviewer_intent.testing: Deep understanding of the thread-local security model and its implications for async code.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Accessing SecurityContextHolder in a @Async method or new Thread and getting null — the child thread has its own empty ThreadLocal.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss MODE_INHERITABLETHREADLOCAL, DelegatingSecurityContextExecutor, and how reactive (WebFlux) Spring Security uses Reactor Context instead of ThreadLocal.

sections.title: SecurityContextHolder Uses ThreadLocal — Which Is Why @Async Methods Get Null Authentication
sections.content:
After authentication succeeds, the `Authentication` object is stored in `SecurityContextHolder`, which by default uses a **`ThreadLocal`** strategy. Every line of code executing on the same thread can access the current user via `SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication()`. When the request completes, the filter chain clears it — deliberately, so the next request on that thread (in a thread pool) starts with an empty context.

The ThreadLocal strategy is invisible and convenient — until you spawn a new thread. **`@Async` methods, `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync()`, and manually created threads each get a fresh ThreadLocal with no security context.** Calling `SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication()` in an async method returns null. If that null authentication reaches an `@PreAuthorize` check, it throws an `InsufficientAuthenticationException` — often surfacing as a confusing 403 in a flow that works perfectly synchronously.

This is one of the most common Spring Security bugs in production: code that works in synchronous controllers fails silently when moved to async processing. The fix depends on the threading model. **`MODE_INHERITABLETHREADLOCAL`** copies the security context to child threads at thread-creation time — safe for `new Thread()`, dangerous for thread pools. **`DelegatingSecurityContextExecutor`** captures the security context at task-submission time and restores it during task execution — safe for thread pools. **Reactor Context** (WebFlux) is a fundamentally different mechanism that replaces ThreadLocal entirely.

sections.title: How Authentication Populates and Clears the SecurityContext Per Request
sections.content:
Tracing what happens to the `SecurityContext` during a single request reveals why the design is the way it is.

**At request entry:** `SecurityContextHolderFilter` runs first. For session-based authentication, it loads the `SecurityContext` from the HTTP session (where it was stored after the last request's login). For stateless JWT APIs, it creates a new empty `SecurityContext`. Either way, `SecurityContextHolder` is initialized before any authentication filter sees the request.

**During authentication:** When a filter like `BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter` validates a JWT, it calls `SecurityContextHolder.getContext().setAuthentication(authentication)`. This stores the `Authentication` — with the principal, cleared credentials, and `GrantedAuthority` list — in the ThreadLocal context. Every subsequent filter and every line of application code on this thread can now access the current user without parameters being passed.

**At request completion:** `SecurityContextHolderFilter`'s finally block calls `SecurityContextHolder.clearContext()`. This removes the `SecurityContext` from the ThreadLocal entirely. Without this clear, the thread returning to the pool would carry the previous request's authentication into the next request — a serious privilege escalation vulnerability. The finally block guarantees the clear happens even if an exception is thrown during the request.

For session-based applications, the `SecurityContext` is persisted to the session (by `HttpSessionSecurityContextRepository`) before the response is committed. The next request restores it from the session in the first step of this cycle.

sections.title: The Async Thread Trap — And the Three Solutions With Their Conditions
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`SecurityContextHolder` is `ThreadLocal` by default** — the `Authentication` stored after login is accessible only on the same thread; `@Async` methods, new `Thread` instances, and reactive code lose the context.
- **`MODE_INHERITABLETHREADLOCAL` propagates to child threads spawned by the current thread** — works for `new Thread()` children but not for thread pool workers (which are not child threads).
- **`DelegatingSecurityContextExecutor` wraps an executor to propagate context** — wraps `ThreadPoolTaskExecutor`; each submitted task gets a copy of the parent thread's `SecurityContext`.
- **Reactive (WebFlux) applications use `ReactorContextWebFilter`** — stores `SecurityContext` in Reactor's `Context`, not `ThreadLocal`; `ReactiveSecurityContextHolder` retrieves it.
- **Clear the `SecurityContext` in finally blocks for non-filter code** — `SecurityContextHolder.clearContext()` after manually setting context prevents security context leakage between requests on pooled threads.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The `SecurityContextHolder` is how Spring Security passes the authenticated user's identity across the layers of your application. The ThreadLocal-based default creates a specific trap in async and multi-threaded code.

**How it works**
- After successful authentication, Spring stores an `Authentication` in the `SecurityContext` held by `SecurityContextHolder`
- Service methods call `SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication()` to get the current user
- At the end of the request, Spring Security clears the context — the ThreadLocal is cleaned up

**The async thread problem**
- `@Async` methods run on a thread pool thread — a different thread from the HTTP request thread
- `SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication()` returns null in `@Async` methods by default
- Fix 1: `SecurityContextHolder.setStrategyName(MODE_INHERITABLETHREADLOCAL)` — child threads inherit context; does not work for thread pool workers
- Fix 2: `DelegatingSecurityContextExecutor` wraps the executor; each task gets a copy of the parent's context — the correct production solution

**WebFlux**
- Reactive code shares no single thread across a request — ThreadLocal would always be empty
- `ReactiveSecurityContextHolder` stores context in Reactor's `Context` (attached to the reactive pipeline)
- `ReactorContextWebFilter` populates it from the session or JWT at the start of each request

questions.question: How do you implement a custom UserDetailsService and UserDetails in Spring Security?
questions.title: UserDetailsService and UserDetails — Custom Implementation
questions.direct_answer: UserDetailsService is a single-method interface that loads user data by username; Spring Security calls it during authentication. UserDetails is an interface describing the loaded user — credentials, account status flags, and granted authorities. You implement both to connect Spring Security to your own database or user store, replacing the default in-memory user management.

sections.title: UserDetailsService Is the Bridge Between Your Database and Spring Security's Authentication Engine
sections.content:
Spring Security doesn't care where your users live — a relational database, LDAP, a REST API, an in-memory map. It only needs one thing: a `UserDetailsService` that takes a username string and returns a `UserDetails` object. **Your entire user model gets filtered through this one-method interface.**

The `UserDetails` contract carries everything Spring Security needs: username, hashed password, four account-status booleans, and a collection of `GrantedAuthority` objects representing roles and permissions. `DaoAuthenticationProvider` calls `loadUserByUsername()`, receives the `UserDetails`, and then uses `PasswordEncoder` to verify the submitted password against the stored hash.

The relationship between `UserDetailsService` and your domain model is intentional separation. Spring Security's authentication engine never sees your `User` entity directly — it sees only `UserDetails`. This means you can evolve your domain model without breaking authentication, and you can provide exactly the subset of user data that authentication needs.

The common mistake surfaces weeks into a project: developers implement the minimum (username, password, one role) and hardcode the four status booleans to return `true`. Later, when the product needs account lockout or forced password expiration, those hardcoded returns mean the security flags do nothing — the column exists in the database, but `isAccountNonLocked()` always returns `true` regardless. **Map these flags to real entity fields from the start**, even if you initialize them all to `true` in the initial migration.

sections.content:
- **`UserDetailsService.loadUserByUsername()` is called on every request when session-based auth is used** — cache the result with `@Cacheable` or in a Redis session to avoid a database query per request.

- **`UserDetailsPasswordService` supports automatic password rehashing** — implement it to upgrade BCrypt work factor on next login without requiring users to reset passwords.
- **`DaoAuthenticationProvider` can be replaced** — implement `AuthenticationProvider` for OAuth2 tokens, LDAP, SAML, or API key authentication; multiple providers are tried in order by `ProviderManager`.

questions.question: What are the trade-offs between session-based and token-based authentication in Spring Security?
questions.title: Session-Based vs Token-Based Authentication
questions.direct_answer: Session-based authentication stores user state server-side in a session tied to a cookie, making revocation instant but requiring sticky sessions or a shared session store in clustered deployments. The right choice depends on scalability requirements and how critical immediate revocation is.

sections.title: JWTs Aren't Always Better — Revocation and Token Size Are Real Problems You'll Hit in Production
sections.content:
Developers default to JWTs because "stateless is better." The missing nuance: stateless means the server **cannot invalidate a token until it expires.** If a user's account is compromised, you cannot force logout — the JWT remains valid until its expiry, potentially for hours or days. Implementing a token blocklist to solve this reintroduces server-side state, which negates much of the stateless advantage. You've now built a worse session system.

Session-based authentication stores only a session ID in the cookie (32 bytes). The server holds the session data — or a shared store like Redis does. The server has full control: `session.invalidate()` immediately renders the session ID useless. The trade-off is that **sessions require coordination** in clustered deployments — either sticky sessions (routing all requests from a user to the same server) or a shared session store (adding a network round-trip per request).

Token-based authentication (JWT) embeds claims in the token itself and sends it on every request. The server validates the signature without server-side storage — no database lookup, no Redis round-trip. The token is self-contained. The real trade-offs that tutorials skip: **JWTs are large** (a typical JWT with roles is 800+ bytes; a session ID is 32 bytes), the payload is encoded (not encrypted, anyone with the token can read the claims), and they can't be revoked.

The choice should follow the architecture. Single-server web app with a database? Sessions are simpler and correct. Microservices where each service independently validates tokens? JWT or opaque tokens with introspection. The trend toward JWT is driven by microservices architectures — not by JWT being inherently superior.

sections.title: Sessions vs JWTs — Every Trade-off That Matters in Production
sections.content:
Neither approach is universally correct. The trade-offs are genuine.

| Aspect | Session-Based | Token-Based (JWT) |
|---|---|---|
| **State location** | Server-side (memory or Redis) | Client-side (inside the token) |
| **Scaling** | Requires sticky sessions or shared store | Stateless — any server validates |
| **Revocation** | Instant — `session.invalidate()` | Not possible without a blocklist |
| **Token size** | 32-byte session ID cookie | 800+ bytes per request |
| **Secret management** | Session store access credentials | Signing key (symmetric or key pair) |
| **XSS risk** | Low — cookie with HttpOnly/Secure | High if stored in localStorage |
| **CSRF risk** | Yes — cookies sent automatically | No — Authorization header requires JS |
| **Cross-domain** | Difficult — cookie domain restrictions | Easy — Authorization header works anywhere |
| **Best for** | Web apps, admin panels, monoliths | APIs, microservices, mobile clients |
| **Spring config** | Default — `SessionCreationPolicy.IF_REQUIRED` | `SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS` |

**The 401 vs 403 distinction disappears** when JWTs expire — an expired token produces 401 (unauthenticated) even if the user's account is active. This is expected but surprises developers who test with long-lived tokens in development and see different behavior in production.

**CSRF and sessions together:** if you store a JWT in a cookie instead of the `Authorization` header, you gain the HttpOnly security benefit but reintroduce CSRF risk — the cookie is sent automatically by the browser. Spring Security's CSRF protection must be re-enabled in this case.

sections.title: Opaque Tokens and Refresh Rotation — When You Need Revocation Without Server-Side Sessions
sections.content:
Sessions and JWTs represent opposite ends of the revocation spectrum. **Opaque tokens** occupy the middle ground that most tutorials ignore.

An opaque token is a random string with no embedded claims — it looks like a session ID. When a resource server receives an opaque token, it sends it to the authorization server's introspection endpoint, which validates the token and returns the associated claims. Revoking an opaque token means marking it invalid at the authorization server — the next introspection call reflects that immediately. This gives you JWT-like stateless APIs (no shared session store between services) with session-like revocation (instant, at the authorization server).

The cost is a network call per authenticated request. Caching introspection responses for 30–60 seconds reduces load while maintaining near-real-time revocation. This is the pattern services like Stripe and Twilio use — tokens are opaque to callers, the authorization server validates them with full revocation support.

**Refresh token rotation** is the practical revocation mechanism within the JWT model. Access tokens expire in 15–30 minutes (short enough that a stolen token has limited window). Refresh tokens are longer-lived but rotate on each use — a new refresh token is issued every time the old one is used. If an attacker steals a refresh token and uses it, the legitimate user's next refresh attempt uses the now-invalidated token, and the server detects the reuse. This is automatic compromise detection with no blocklist needed.

My recommendation: use sessions for web applications where server control matters; use JWTs with short expiry and refresh rotation for APIs; consider opaque tokens when you're running an OAuth2 authorization server that needs API-level revocation control.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Sessions are server-side state; tokens are client-side state** — sessions require shared storage (Redis) in multi-instance deployments; tokens (JWT) are self-contained and require no server state.
- **JWTs cannot be revoked before expiry without a blocklist** — a stolen JWT is valid until its `exp` claim; implement a Redis blocklist of revoked token IDs to enable logout and revocation.
- **JWT payload is base64-encoded, not encrypted** — anyone can decode the payload without the signing key; never put passwords, PII, or sensitive data in JWT claims.
- **Opaque tokens with introspection are a middle ground** — the token is a random string stored in Redis; every request introspects it (one Redis lookup per request); revocable without a blocklist.
- **`SameSite=Strict` on session cookies prevents CSRF without CSRF tokens** — modern browsers refuse to send `SameSite=Strict` cookies on cross-origin requests, eliminating the attack vector.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Session-based and token-based authentication have fundamentally different scaling and revocation characteristics. Choosing between them is an architectural decision, not just a library choice.

**Session-based (stateful)**
- User logs in; server creates a session and stores it (in memory or Redis); client gets a session cookie
- On each request, the server looks up the session in storage to authenticate
- Revocation is instant — delete the session from storage
- Requires sticky sessions or shared storage (Redis) in multi-instance deployments

**JWT-based (stateless)**
- User logs in; server issues a signed JWT; client stores it and sends it in `Authorization: Bearer` header
- On each request, the server verifies the signature — no storage lookup
- Scales horizontally with no shared state between instances
- Revocation requires a blocklist (Redis set of revoked JTI claims) — adds a storage lookup per request

**The JWT payload is not secret**
- Base64 decoding reveals the payload — it is signed, not encrypted
- Do not put sensitive data in claims; use a separate endpoint to fetch user details if needed

**Opaque tokens**
- Random string stored server-side (Redis); each request exchanges it for user data via introspection
- Instantly revocable; one Redis lookup per request — the performance trade-off between sessions and JWTs

sections.title: Building JWT Auth Without Understanding the Security Implications Is Worse Than Using Sessions
sections.content:
Implementing JWT authentication in Spring Security is mechanically straightforward — generate a token at login, validate it on every request. The security mistakes are where real applications break. **Storing tokens in localStorage exposes them to XSS** — any JavaScript on the page (including injected malicious scripts) can read `localStorage`. **Forgetting `sessionCreationPolicy(STATELESS)`** means Spring creates sessions alongside JWT, wasting memory and misleading developers who think session-based revocation is working. **Using a weak HS256 secret** makes tokens forgeable by anyone who can brute-force the key.

Before writing a custom implementation, consider Spring Security 6's built-in OAuth2 Resource Server support (`spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server`). **For most applications that validate tokens but don't issue them**, the built-in support requires zero custom filter code — just configuration. The custom implementation path is for applications that ARE the token issuer (not using Keycloak, Auth0, or another external authorization server).

The complete custom implementation has four components:
- A `JwtUtil` class for token generation and validation (wrapping a JWT library like `jjwt` or `nimbus-jose-jwt`)
- A `OncePerRequestFilter` subclass that extracts and validates the token on each request
- A login endpoint that calls `AuthenticationManager`, generates the token on success, and returns it
- A `SecurityFilterChain` that disables sessions, disables CSRF, registers the filter, and protects endpoints

Each of these has a failure mode that's easy to miss.

sections.title: Token Generation at Login — Claims, Signing Algorithm, and Expiry Strategy
The Authentication Filter — Validating Tokens on Every Request Without Hitting the Database
SecurityFilterChain Configuration — Three Settings That Must All Be Correct
sections.content:
The security configuration ties the pieces together. Three settings are all essential and all easy to get wrong:

```java
@Bean
public SecurityFilterChain securityFilterChain(HttpSecurity http,
                                               JwtAuthFilter jwtAuthFilter) throws Exception {
    return http
        .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())            // safe — no session cookies to exploit
        .sessionManagement(session -> session
            .sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))  // no sessions
        .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
            .requestMatchers("/auth/login", "/auth/register").permitAll()
            .anyRequest().authenticated())
        .addFilterBefore(jwtAuthFilter, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class)
        .build();
}
```

**`SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS`** prevents Spring Security from creating HTTP sessions. Without this, every authenticated request creates a session object. The session does nothing useful (JWT is stateless), but it consumes memory. On a busy server handling 1000 requests/second, this adds significant garbage collection pressure.

**`csrf.disable()`** is safe because JWT tokens in the `Authorization` header cannot be included in cross-site requests — browsers don't automatically attach headers the way they attach cookies. If you later move JWT storage to an HttpOnly cookie instead of the `Authorization` header, you must re-enable CSRF. This is a nuanced decision that the `to_stand_out` guidance highlights.

**`addFilterBefore`** placement is critical. The JWT filter must run before `UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter` to populate the `SecurityContext` before authorization decisions are made. The filter is registered as a bean — no `@Component` needed; registering it in the `SecurityFilterChain` is sufficient and prevents it from being applied twice (Spring Boot auto-registers all `Filter` beans, which would double-apply this filter without the exclusion).

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **JWT filter must run before `UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter`** — use `addFilterBefore(jwtFilter, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class)` so the JWT is parsed and the `SecurityContext` is populated before the standard auth filter runs.
- **Store JWTs in `httpOnly` cookies, not `localStorage`** — `httpOnly` cookies are inaccessible to JavaScript, preventing XSS theft; `localStorage` is vulnerable to any script running on the page.
- **Short `exp` + refresh token rotation** — access token TTL: 15 minutes; refresh token: 7-30 days in `httpOnly` cookie; rotation: issue a new refresh token on each use and invalidate the old one.
- **Verify `alg`, `iss`, `aud` claims** — a JWT with `alg: none` has no signature; verify the algorithm matches your expected one; `iss` and `aud` claims bind the token to the expected issuer and audience.
- **Do not store user data in the JWT** — the payload is base64-visible; store only `sub` (user ID), `iss`, `exp`, `iat`, and required authorization claims; fetch sensitive user data by ID from a service.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Implementing JWT authentication in Spring Security means writing a custom filter that validates the token and populates the `SecurityContext` before the rest of the filter chain runs.

**The filter implementation**
- Extend `OncePerRequestFilter`
- Extract `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header
- Validate the JWT: signature, `exp`, `alg`, `iss`, `aud`
- Load `UserDetails` by the `sub` claim and create a `UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken`
- Set it in `SecurityContextHolder.getContext().setAuthentication(auth)`
- Register: `http.addFilterBefore(jwtFilter, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class)`

**Token storage**
- `httpOnly` cookie — inaccessible to JavaScript; XSS-safe; needs CSRF protection if used with session cookies
- `localStorage` — vulnerable to XSS; any script on the page can read and send the token
- For SPAs: short-lived access token in memory + long-lived refresh token in `httpOnly` cookie

**Refresh token rotation**
- Access token: 15-minute TTL; client refreshes silently when expired
- Refresh token: 7-day TTL stored in `httpOnly` cookie; on use, issue a new refresh token and revoke the old one
- Rotation limits the window of damage if a refresh token is stolen — re-use of a revoked token signals theft

sections.title: A JWT Signed With 'none' Is an Unsigned Postcard — Anyone Can Write Anything On It
sections.content:
JWT security has multiple layers, and each one has a known attack vector. The **algorithm confusion attack** is the most subtle: some JWT libraries accept the algorithm from the token's own header without validation. An attacker takes a valid RS256 token, changes the `alg` header to `HS256`, and signs the modified payload with the server's public key — which is, by definition, publicly available. If the library uses whatever algorithm the token header specifies and treats the public key as the HS256 symmetric secret, the forged token validates. The fix is simple but must be explicit: **always enforce the expected algorithm server-side** and never trust the `alg` header from an incoming token.

The `none` algorithm disables signature verification entirely. A token with `"alg": "none"` carries no signature — anyone can modify the payload. Modern libraries reject `none` by default, but older versions and misconfigured setups don't. Always configure your JWT validator with a specific expected algorithm and reject anything else.

**Expiry management is the second critical concern.** JWTs cannot be revoked until they expire — this is the fundamental statelessness trade-off. A 24-hour access token means a stolen token is usable for up to 24 hours with no recourse. **Short-lived access tokens (15–30 minutes)** paired with **longer-lived refresh tokens** (days, stored in HttpOnly cookies) balance security with usability. The access token's short life limits the stolen-token window. The refresh token, stored HttpOnly, is not accessible to JavaScript.

**Token storage determines XSS exposure.** `localStorage` is readable by any JavaScript on the page — one XSS vulnerability means all tokens are stolen. HttpOnly cookies are never accessible from JavaScript. The browser attaches them automatically, which reintroduces CSRF risk (but CSRF is manageable with `SameSite=Lax` or CSRF tokens). For browser clients, HttpOnly cookie storage is the stronger security choice.

sections.title: HS256 vs RS256 — Choosing the Right Signing Algorithm
sections.content:
The signing algorithm determines how tokens are verified and who can do it.

| Aspect | HS256 (HMAC-SHA256) | RS256 (RSA-SHA256) |
|---|---|---|
| **Key type** | Symmetric — one secret for both signing and verification | Asymmetric — private key signs, public key verifies |
| **Key sharing** | Every service that validates tokens needs the secret | Only the auth server needs the private key |
| **Key compromise risk** | Single secret compromise breaks everything | Private key stays on auth server; public key is safe to share |
| **Performance** | Faster — HMAC hash operation | Slower — RSA cryptographic operation |
| **JWKS support** | Not standard | Yes — public key published at `/.well-known/jwks.json` |
| **Multi-service** | Secret must be securely distributed to each service | Public key distributed freely; no security risk |
| **Best for** | Single service, controlled environment | Microservices, OAuth2, public APIs |

HS256 is simpler and faster. The problem is **secret distribution** — every service that validates tokens must have the same secret, and that secret must be kept secure everywhere it exists. In microservices with ten services validating tokens, you have ten places where the secret can leak.

RS256 solves distribution: the private key never leaves the authorization server. Resource servers download the public key from the JWKS endpoint and cache it. No secret to share, no secret to accidentally commit to Git, no secret to rotate across ten services simultaneously. **Use RS256 for any multi-service architecture.** HS256 is acceptable only for monoliths or tightly controlled single-service environments.

Key rotation: RS256 keys can be rotated by publishing a new key at the JWKS endpoint. JWTs include a `kid` (key ID) claim that tells the validator which key to use for verification, enabling seamless rotation without service restarts.

sections.title: Refresh Token Rotation and Token Blocklists — Production Patterns for the Revocation Problem
sections.content:
JWT's fundamental limitation is the inability to revoke tokens before expiry. Two production patterns address this without abandoning statelessness.

**Refresh token rotation** provides automatic compromise detection. On every refresh operation, the server issues a new refresh token and invalidates the old one. Store refresh tokens in the database with a status flag. If an attacker steals a refresh token and uses it first, the legitimate user's next refresh attempt presents the old (now-invalidated) token — the server detects the reuse and can invalidate the entire session. The user gets logged out; the attacker's stolen token stops working. This is proactive compromise detection without a blocklist for access tokens.

For logout and account compromise scenarios, a **token blocklist** in Redis handles access token revocation. The `jti` (JWT ID) claim uniquely identifies each token — add it at token generation time with `UUID.randomUUID().toString()`. On logout, store the `jti` in Redis with a TTL matching the token's remaining validity. On each request, check the `jti` against Redis before accepting the token.

The blocklist remains small because entries expire naturally: a 15-minute access token's blocklist entry exists for at most 15 minutes. Redis TTL handles cleanup automatically. For a service with 10,000 concurrent users and 15-minute access tokens, the blocklist holds at most 10,000 entries — trivial for Redis.

**Never store sensitive data in JWT claims.** The payload is Base64URL-encoded, not encrypted. Any holder of the token can decode the payload with `atob()` in JavaScript or any base64 decoder. Store only identifiers (user ID), roles, and non-sensitive metadata. PII, financial data, or internal system identifiers must never appear in JWT claims.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **HS256 (symmetric) vs RS256/ES256 (asymmetric)** — HS256: same secret signs and verifies; all parties need the secret; RS256: private key signs, public key verifies; resource servers only need the public key.
- **Algorithm confusion attack: never trust `alg` from the token header** — `alg: none` disables signature verification; explicitly specify the expected algorithm in your JWT library, never accept what the token declares.
- **Short expiry + refresh token rotation prevents long-window compromise** — access token: 15 min; a stolen token expires quickly; refresh token rotation (invalidate on use) detects theft by re-use.
- **Token blacklisting with Redis JTI** — store `jti` (JWT ID) of revoked tokens in Redis with TTL matching the token's remaining valid time; check on every request; enables logout and forced revocation.
- **`nbf` (not before) and `iat` (issued at) claims prevent replay** — validate `nbf` ≤ current time ≤ `exp`; validate `iat` is not in the future; reject tokens with implausible timestamps.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
JWT security goes beyond 'validate the signature'. The real risks are algorithm confusion, long-lived tokens, and the inability to revoke without a blocklist.

**Signing algorithm choice**
- **HS256** (HMAC-SHA256): symmetric — same secret for signing and verification; all services that verify tokens must share the secret; simpler for single-service setups
- **RS256** (RSA-SHA256): asymmetric — authorization server signs with private key; resource servers verify with public key from JWKS endpoint; private key never leaves the auth server
- **ES256** (ECDSA-SHA256): asymmetric, smaller key size, faster than RSA; increasingly preferred

**Algorithm confusion attack**
- An attacker crafts a token with `{"alg": "none"}` — no signature needed
- Vulnerable libraries accept it if they derive the algorithm from the token header
- Fix: always specify the expected algorithm explicitly in your JWT library configuration

**Expiry strategy**
- Access token: 15-minute TTL — short window of exposure
- Refresh token: 7-30 day TTL, stored in `httpOnly` cookie
- Refresh token rotation: every use issues a new refresh token and revokes the old; re-use of a revoked token is a theft signal → revoke the entire family

**Revocation**
- Store revoked `jti` values in Redis with TTL = remaining valid time of the token
- Check on every request — one Redis lookup; enables instant logout and compromise response

questions.title: OAuth2 Authorization Code Flow
questions.direct_answer: The OAuth2 authorization code flow separates user authentication from token issuance by using a short-lived authorization code as an intermediary. The browser never receives the access token directly — it is exchanged server-to-server after the code is received. This prevents tokens from being exposed in browser history, logs, or referrer headers.

sections.title: The Authorization Code Flow Exists Because Browsers Are Not Safe Places for Access Tokens
sections.content:
Before the authorization code flow existed, OAuth implementations used the **implicit flow**: the authorization server returned the access token directly in the URL fragment (`#access_token=...`) after authentication. The problem: URL fragments appear in browser history, server access logs, referrer headers sent to third-party resources embedded in the page, and anywhere else URLs are recorded. A token in the URL is a token that has been logged in six places.

The authorization code flow solves this by using **an intermediate short-lived code** instead of the token. The code appears in the URL — it can be logged — but it's useless without the client secret and expires in 60 seconds. The actual access token is obtained via a back-channel server-to-server request that never touches the browser. Browsers never see the access token.

The flow also solves the **client verification problem**. When the authorization server issues a code, it records which redirect URI was used. The client must present the same redirect URI during token exchange. Combined with the client secret (for confidential clients), this proves that the entity exchanging the code is the same registered client that started the flow — not an attacker who intercepted the code.

**Spring Security OAuth2 Client** handles the entire flow automatically. After configuring `spring.security.oauth2.client.registration.*` properties and calling `.oauth2Login()` in the security configuration, Spring manages the redirect, state parameter, code reception, token exchange, token storage, and refresh — without any custom code. Understanding the flow is essential for debugging it when it breaks.

sections.title: Authorization Request and User Authentication — The Client Steps Out of the Way
sections.content:
The flow begins when the client application redirects the user's browser to the authorization server's `/authorize` endpoint. The redirect URL includes: `response_type=code`, `client_id`, `redirect_uri` (must match what's registered), `scope` (what permissions are requested), and `state`.

**The `state` parameter** is the CSRF protection mechanism for OAuth2 itself. The client generates a cryptographically random value, stores it in the session, and sends it with the authorization request. When the authorization server redirects back, it includes the same `state`. The client validates that the received value matches the stored one before processing the code. Without this check, an attacker can craft a redirect URL that triggers the flow and associates their account with the victim's — a flow-injection attack that's subtle and devastating.

After redirecting the user, the client waits. The authorization server runs its own authentication flow — login form, SSO, MFA, biometrics — entirely independent of the client. **The client has zero involvement in how the user authenticates.** This is the key delegation principle: the client trusts the authorization server to verify identity, and the authorization server trusts the client to use the token only for what it's permitted.

If authentication succeeds and the user consents to the requested scopes, the authorization server redirects to the client's `redirect_uri` with `code=<short-lived-code>&state=<original-state>`. The code is typically valid for 60 seconds and can only be used once — a used or expired code is immediately rejected.

sections.title: Back-Channel Token Exchange — Why Tokens Never Touch the Browser
sections.content:
The authorization code visible in the browser URL and potentially logged in several places is not the access token. It's a limited-time, single-use voucher that the server exchanges for tokens in a back-channel request.

The client's backend (not the browser, not JavaScript) sends a POST to the authorization server's `/token` endpoint with: `grant_type=authorization_code`, the received `code`, `redirect_uri` (must match exactly), `client_id`, and `client_secret` (for confidential clients). The authorization server validates all fields — mismatched redirect URI or wrong client secret causes immediate rejection.

On success, the response includes: an `access_token` (short-lived, used for API calls), optionally a `refresh_token` (longer-lived, for obtaining new access tokens), and for OIDC flows, an `id_token` (a JWT containing user identity claims for the client). **Access tokens authorize API calls. ID tokens identify the user to the client.** They're different tokens for different purposes — a common confusion point.

The access token and refresh token are returned in the response body of a server-to-server HTTP call. They never appear in a URL, never appear in browser history, and never appear in referrer headers. The back-channel exchange is the security guarantee of this flow. An attacker who intercepts the authorization code from a URL still can't exchange it — they lack the client secret or PKCE verifier.

**Spring Security OAuth2 Client** stores the obtained tokens in the `OAuth2AuthorizedClient`, accessible via `@RegisteredOAuth2AuthorizedClient` in controller methods. Spring also handles token refresh automatically when the access token expires, using the stored refresh token.

sections.title: PKCE — Extending the Flow to Public Clients Without a Client Secret
sections.content:
Confidential clients (web server applications) can keep a client secret secure. Public clients — single-page applications, mobile apps — cannot. A client secret embedded in a JavaScript bundle or mobile app binary is not secret; it's accessible to anyone who inspects the bundle.

**PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange)** removes the need for a client secret by using a cryptographic challenge. The client generates a random 43–128 character `code_verifier`. It computes `code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(code_verifier))` and sends the challenge with the authorization request. During token exchange, it sends the original `code_verifier`. The authorization server hashes the verifier and compares it to the stored challenge — if they match, the exchange is legitimate.

An attacker who intercepts the authorization code cannot exchange it — they have the code and the challenge (from the authorization request), but not the `code_verifier` that only the legitimate client generated and never transmitted publicly. PKCE provides the same binding as a client secret without requiring a shared secret.

**OAuth 2.1 (the current draft successor) requires PKCE for all clients**, not just public clients, because PKCE also prevents authorization code injection attacks even for confidential clients. Spring Security OAuth2 Client supports PKCE transparently for registered clients configured with `client-authentication-method=none`. The `code_verifier` generation, challenge computation, and verification are handled automatically.

**OIDC adds the ID token** to the authorization code flow response. The ID token is a JWT signed by the authorization server containing the user's identity claims: `sub` (subject/user ID), `email`, `name`, and any other requested profile claims. The access token authorizes API calls; the ID token identifies the user. Both are issued in the same token exchange response.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Authorization code flow: the token never passes through the browser URL** — the browser receives an authorization code (short-lived, one-use); the backend exchanges it for tokens via a server-to-server call.
- **PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) is mandatory for public clients (SPAs, mobile)** — the client generates a `code_verifier`, sends the hash (`code_challenge`) with the authorization request; proves the exchanger is the same party that initiated the flow.
- **`state` parameter prevents CSRF on the authorization endpoint** — the client generates a random `state`, sends it with the authorization request, and validates it in the callback; a missing or mismatched `state` indicates CSRF.
- **`access_token` is short-lived; `refresh_token` is long-lived** — access tokens are bearer tokens (no server lookup); refresh tokens are opaque and revocable at the authorization server.
- **Spring Boot OAuth2 Client auto-configures the flow** — `spring-boot-starter-oauth2-client` + `spring.security.oauth2.client.registration.*` properties handle redirect, code exchange, token storage, and token refresh automatically.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
OAuth2 authorization code flow is the standard for 'Login with Google/GitHub/Microsoft' and for delegated access between services. Understanding each step is a common interview question for senior backend roles.

**The flow — step by step**
1. User clicks 'Login with Google'; your app redirects to `https://accounts.google.com/o/oauth2/auth?client_id=...&redirect_uri=...&state=<random>&scope=openid email`
2. User authenticates at Google and approves the scopes
3. Google redirects back to your `redirect_uri` with `?code=<auth_code>&state=<same_random>`
4. Your backend verifies `state` matches, then exchanges `code` for tokens via POST to Google's token endpoint — server-to-server, the code never touches the browser again
5. Google returns `access_token` (short-lived) + `id_token` (JWT with user info) + `refresh_token`
6. Your app stores tokens and uses `access_token` to call Google APIs on the user's behalf

**Why authorization code instead of implicit flow**
- Implicit flow returned the access token in the URL fragment — visible in browser history, referrer headers, and logs
- Authorization code flow: the token is exchanged server-to-server; the browser only sees a one-time code

**PKCE for SPAs**
- SPAs cannot keep a client secret; PKCE proves the code exchanger is the same origin that initiated the flow
- Required for any public client (no client secret) using authorization code flow

questions.title: OAuth2 Resource Server Configuration in Spring Security
questions.direct_answer: A Resource Server validates JWT Bearer tokens on incoming requests to protect API endpoints. Spring Security's built-in OAuth2 Resource Server support requires adding the spring-security-oauth2-resource-server dependency, providing the JWK Set URI (so Spring can fetch the authorization server's public keys), and calling .oauth2ResourceServer() in the SecurityFilterChain. Spring handles JWT validation, claim extraction, and GrantedAuthority mapping automatically.

sections.title: Stop Writing Custom JWT Filters — Spring Security's Resource Server Does It More Securely and With Less Code
sections.content:
The most common mistake when implementing JWT-protected APIs is writing a custom `OncePerRequestFilter` that manually parses the `Authorization` header, validates the signature, and sets the `Authentication`. Developers copy this pattern from tutorials and end up with custom JWT parsing code that misses edge cases: algorithm confusion attacks, key rotation, audience validation, and clock skew handling.

**Spring Security's OAuth2 Resource Server handles all of this with two lines of configuration.** Add `spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server` and set `spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri`. Spring Security downloads the JWK Set (the authorization server's public keys) from the OIDC discovery endpoint, caches them, validates every JWT's signature and expiry, checks the `iss` claim against the configured issuer, and creates a `JwtAuthenticationToken` — all automatically. No custom filter, no JWT library dependency, no signature validation code to maintain.

The one customization almost every application needs is **claim-to-authority mapping**. By default, Spring Security reads the `scope` claim and creates authorities prefixed with `SCOPE_`. Most applications use a `roles` claim with `ROLE_` prefixed authorities. This mismatch is silent: authentication succeeds, `JwtAuthenticationToken` is populated, but `hasRole("ADMIN")` fails because Spring Security is looking for `ROLE_ADMIN` and finding only `SCOPE_ADMIN` or finding the claim under the wrong key. A `JwtAuthenticationConverter` bean fixes this — it's the most common first configuration step after getting the basic setup working.

sections.title: Minimal Resource Server Configuration — Two Lines That Enable Full JWT Validation
sections.content:
The minimum working configuration requires only a dependency and a property.

In `application.yml`:
```yaml
spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      resourceserver:
        jwt:
          issuer-uri: https://auth-server.example.com
```

In the security configuration:
```java
@Bean
public SecurityFilterChain filterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http
        .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
            .requestMatchers("/public/**").permitAll()
            .anyRequest().authenticated())
        .oauth2ResourceServer(oauth2 -> oauth2
            .jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()))   // enables JWT Bearer token validation
        .build();
}
```

With `issuer-uri`, Spring Security fetches `https://auth-server.example.com/.well-known/openid-configuration` at startup, discovers the JWK Set URI, downloads the public keys, and validates the `iss` claim in every token against the configured value. Tokens from other issuers are rejected. Use `jwk-set-uri` (the raw JWK Set URL) instead of `issuer-uri` if the authorization server doesn't have an OIDC discovery endpoint — but you lose the issuer claim validation.

The resulting `JwtAuthenticationToken` is available in controllers via `@AuthenticationPrincipal Jwt jwt` — the full JWT object with all claims. Access `jwt.getClaimAsString("sub")` for the subject, `jwt.getClaimAsStringList("roles")` for roles, and so on. Spring Security manages key rotation automatically — when the authorization server adds a new key to the JWK Set, Spring fetches and caches the updated set on the next validation that encounters an unknown `kid` claim.

sections.title: Custom Claim Mapping — Fixing the SCOPE_ vs ROLE_ Mismatch
Opaque Tokens, Multi-Tenancy, and Advanced JWT Decoder Configuration
sections.content:
For opaque tokens (random strings with no embedded claims), configure the introspection endpoint instead of the JWK Set URI:

```yaml
spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.opaquetoken.introspection-uri=https://auth.example.com/introspect
spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.opaquetoken.client-id=resource-server
spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.opaquetoken.client-secret=secret
```

Spring Security calls the introspection endpoint on every request with the token, receiving `active: true/false` and the associated claims. The key trade-off: **opaque tokens support instant revocation** (the authorization server checks validity on each introspection) but add a **network round-trip per request**. Cache introspection responses for 30–60 seconds to reduce the performance impact while maintaining near-real-time revocation.

For **multi-tenant applications** serving tokens from multiple authorization servers (different Okta tenants, internal and external IdPs), configure `JwtIssuerAuthenticationManagerResolver`:

```java
@Bean
public JwtIssuerAuthenticationManagerResolver authenticationManagerResolver() {
    // Spring fetches JWK Sets for each trusted issuer separately
    return JwtIssuerAuthenticationManagerResolver
        .fromTrustedIssuers("https://issuer1.example.com", "https://issuer2.example.com");
}
```

This reads the `iss` claim from each incoming JWT without verifying the signature first, looks up the configured `JwtDecoder` for that issuer, and delegates validation. The list of trusted issuers is your allowlist — an `iss` claim not in that list results in immediate rejection. Never build this allowlist from user input or token claims — hardcode or load from configuration only.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Resource server validates the JWT — it does not issue it** — the authorization server issues tokens; the resource server (your API) only validates the signature and claims using the public key from the JWKS endpoint.
- **`spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server` + `issuer-uri` property is the minimal configuration** — Spring auto-fetches the JWKS from `{issuer-uri}/.well-known/openid-configuration` and validates every `Authorization: Bearer` request.
- **Custom `JwtAuthenticationConverter` maps JWT claims to `GrantedAuthority`** — the default maps `scope` claims; override to map custom claims (`roles`, `permissions`) to Spring's `GrantedAuthority` list.
- **`JwtDecoder` can be customized for additional claim validation** — validate `aud` (audience), `iss` (issuer), custom business claims; `NimbusJwtDecoder.withJwkSetUri()` + `.jwtProcessorCustomizer()` for extra validators.
- **Opaque token introspection for non-JWT tokens** — `spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.opaquetoken.introspection-uri` configures a resource server that calls the auth server on every request to validate the token.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
A resource server is any API that accepts OAuth2 tokens to authorize requests. Spring Security's resource server support validates JWTs without writing any filter code.

**Minimal setup**
```yaml
spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      resourceserver:
        jwt:
          issuer-uri: https://auth.example.com
```
- Spring fetches the JWKS URI from the issuer's `.well-known/openid-configuration`
- Every request with `Authorization: Bearer <jwt>` is validated against the fetched public keys
- Claims are mapped to a `JwtAuthenticationToken` in the `SecurityContext`

**Mapping claims to authorities**
- Default: Spring maps `scope` claims to `SCOPE_read`, `SCOPE_write` authorities
- Custom: `@Bean JwtAuthenticationConverter` — extract a custom `roles` claim and map to `ROLE_ADMIN`, `ROLE_USER`
- `@PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('SCOPE_read')")` or `hasRole('ADMIN')` — depends on how you mapped

**Additional claim validation**
- Validate `aud` claim: `OAuth2TokenValidator<Jwt>` that checks `jwt.getAudience().contains("my-api")`
- Compose with `DelegatingOAuth2TokenValidator` to run multiple validators
- Fails validation → `401 Unauthorized` with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token"`

questions.question: What are the differences between @PreAuthorize, @Secured, and @RolesAllowed in Spring Security?
questions.title: @PreAuthorize vs @Secured vs @RolesAllowed
questions.direct_answer: @PreAuthorize is the most powerful — it accepts Spring Expression Language (SpEL) and can inspect method arguments, return values, and bean state. @Secured accepts a simple list of role strings and predates SpEL. @RolesAllowed is the JSR-250 standard annotation, also role-string only. For any non-trivial authorization logic, @PreAuthorize is the preferred modern choice.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of method security options and when to use SpEL expressions vs simple role checks.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @Secured or @RolesAllowed and then discovering they cannot express 'only the owner of this resource can edit it' — that requires SpEL in @PreAuthorize.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention @PostAuthorize for filtering return values, @PreFilter/@PostFilter for collections, and that method security requires @EnableMethodSecurity (not @EnableGlobalMethodSecurity in Spring Security 6).

sections.title: @Secured Can't Express 'Only the Owner Can Edit' — @PreAuthorize With SpEL Can
sections.content:
Most developers start with `@Secured("ROLE_ADMIN")` because it looks simple and clean. Then the product requirement arrives: "only the owner can edit their own order." **`@Secured` and `@RolesAllowed` cannot express this.** They accept a list of role strings and perform a simple role membership check — nothing more. Resource-level authorization that depends on the relationship between the authenticated user and the specific data being accessed is impossible with these annotations.

**`@PreAuthorize`** accepts SpEL expressions with access to the method's parameters, the authenticated principal, and Spring-managed beans. `@PreAuthorize("#order.userId == authentication.principal.id")` checks that the order belongs to the current user. `@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN') or @orderService.isOwner(#orderId, authentication)")` combines a role check with a service-level ownership check. The `@orderService` bean call is the key capability — you can implement any authorization logic as a Spring bean method and invoke it from the SpEL expression.

The migration from `@EnableGlobalMethodSecurity` (deprecated in Spring Security 6) to `@EnableMethodSecurity` is not optional for new code. The old annotation enabled method security through a voter-based system and required explicit flags (`prePostEnabled=true`). The new annotation enables `@PreAuthorize` by default and uses the cleaner `AuthorizationManager` architecture. Getting this wrong means `@PreAuthorize` silently has no effect — authorization appears to work because no exception is thrown, but all access is permitted. Test your method security annotations.

sections.title: Three Annotations Compared — Capability, SpEL Support, and Enable Configuration
sections.content:
The decision matrix is straightforward once you know what each annotation can express.

| Aspect | @Secured | @RolesAllowed | @PreAuthorize |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Standard** | Spring-specific | JSR-250 (Jakarta EE) | Spring-specific |
| **SpEL expressions** | No | No | Yes — full Spring Expression Language |
| **Role checks** | Yes | Yes | Yes — `hasRole()`, `hasAuthority()` |
| **Parameter access** | No | No | Yes — `#paramName` |
| **Principal access** | No | No | Yes — `authentication.principal.id` |
| **Custom beans** | No | No | Yes — `@beanName.method()` in expression |
| **Post-execution filter** | No | No | Yes — `@PostAuthorize`, `@PostFilter` |
| **Enable with** | `@EnableMethodSecurity(securedEnabled=true)` | `@EnableMethodSecurity(jsr250Enabled=true)` | `@EnableMethodSecurity` (default on) |
| **Spring Security 6 status** | Supported | Supported | Preferred |

**`@PostAuthorize`** evaluates after the method executes and can access the return value via `returnObject`. `@PostAuthorize("returnObject.userId == authentication.principal.id")` ensures a `findById()` call doesn't return another user's data — the method runs, but the result is blocked if the condition fails. **`@PreFilter`** and **`@PostFilter`** apply to collections: `@PreFilter` removes input collection elements that don't satisfy the expression before the method runs; `@PostFilter` removes output elements after.

These post-execution annotations enable **data-level security** without changing every repository method — a powerful pattern for multi-tenant applications where every user should see only their own data.

sections.title: Which Annotation to Use — The Decision Is Simpler Than the Documentation Suggests
sections.content:
**Use `@PreAuthorize` for everything new.** It covers every case that `@Secured` and `@RolesAllowed` cover, plus resource ownership, parameter-based access, and post-execution filtering. The only reason to reach for `@Secured` or `@RolesAllowed` is maintaining consistency in a codebase that already uses them extensively.

For simple role checks, `@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")` is slightly more verbose than `@Secured("ROLE_ADMIN")` but provides a consistent pattern throughout the codebase — reviewers don't need to remember which annotation supports which features. `hasRole('ADMIN')` vs `hasAuthority('ROLE_ADMIN')` is worth knowing: `hasRole()` automatically prepends `ROLE_`; `hasAuthority()` checks the exact string. For custom authorities without the `ROLE_` prefix, use `hasAuthority()`.

When SpEL expressions become complex — `@PreAuthorize("hasRole('MANAGER') and @projectService.isTeamMember(#projectId, authentication) and @planLimits.withinQuota(authentication)")` — extract the logic into a custom `PermissionEvaluator` or a dedicated authorization service bean. Complex SpEL expressions are hard to test, hard to audit, and silently do nothing if misconfigured. A testable service method `@PreAuthorize("@authService.canAccess(#projectId, authentication)")` is cleaner and the logic is unit-testable independently.

Enable everything with `@EnableMethodSecurity` on any `@Configuration` class. Add `prePostEnabled=true` is not needed — it's the default. Add `securedEnabled=true` or `jsr250Enabled=true` only if you need those annotation types alongside `@PreAuthorize`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@PreAuthorize` supports SpEL expressions; `@Secured` and `@RolesAllowed` do not** — `@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN') or #userId == authentication.name")` uses method parameters in the expression; `@Secured` and `@RolesAllowed` only accept role string literals.
- **`@EnableMethodSecurity` replaces `@EnableGlobalMethodSecurity`** — Spring Security 6.x; `@EnableMethodSecurity(prePostEnabled = true)` enables `@PreAuthorize`/`@PostAuthorize`; the old annotation is deprecated.
- **`@PostAuthorize` evaluates after the method returns** — check if the returned object belongs to the current user: `@PostAuthorize("returnObject.ownerId == authentication.name")`.
- **`@PreFilter` and `@PostFilter` filter collections** — `@PreFilter("filterObject.userId == authentication.name")` removes elements from the input list that the user does not own before the method runs.
- **Method security works through AOP proxies — self-invocation bypasses it** — `this.securedMethod()` inside the same class skips the security proxy; extract to a separate Spring bean.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring Security offers three annotation styles for method-level authorization. Knowing which to use — and why the others exist — shows depth.

**`@PreAuthorize` — the standard choice**
- `@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")` — simple role check
- `@PreAuthorize("hasRole('USER') and #id == authentication.name")` — the `#id` references the method parameter named `id`
- Evaluated before the method runs; access denied before any business logic executes

**`@PostAuthorize` — for ownership checks on return values**
- `@PostAuthorize("returnObject.ownerId == authentication.name")`
- The method runs first, then the expression is evaluated against the return value
- Use when you cannot determine authorization without knowing the result

**`@Secured` and `@RolesAllowed`**
- `@Secured({"ROLE_ADMIN", "ROLE_MANAGER"})` — Spring-specific; role string literals only
- `@RolesAllowed("ADMIN")` — JSR-250; Java standard; role strings only
- Both lack SpEL; use `@PreAuthorize` for anything beyond a simple role list

**Self-invocation trap**
- Method security is AOP-based; calling `this.method()` bypasses the proxy and skips security
- Always inject the bean and call through the proxy for method security to work
